The storm had been raging for three days, a relentless assault of wind and rain that battered the granite cliffs of Blackwood Point. Elias, the keeper, moved with the quiet efficiency of a man who had lived within these walls for forty years. He climbed the spiral staircase, his boots heavy with salt and damp wool, checking the oil levels in the great lens. The mechanism hummed, a steady, rhythmic pulse against the chaos outside.

At the base of the tower, the world was a churning abyss of black water and white foam. But up here, in the glass cage, there was only light. Elias polished the brass fittings until they gleamed, a ritual as sacred as prayer. He thought of the ships navigating the dark, their crews trusting this single, unwavering beam to guide them through the treacherous shoals. It was a lonely existence, but not a silent one. The wind sang in the rigging, the waves crashed against the foundation, and the clock ticked, marking time in the void.

One night, a distress flare bloomed red against the storm’s gray curtain. Elias watched it from the gallery, his heart tightening. He adjusted the rotation speed, ensuring the light swept faster, more urgently. He spoke
